_comment: eBird/Clements 2025 corrections to the ACO 2022 base list (docs/DECISIONS.md row 19). `species`: Clements 2025 species absent from ACO 2022 (post-2022 splits) that GBIF/eBird records at route sites; common.checklist() adds them to the ACO list with `source: clements2025`, so ebird/birdbase/wikidata/build pick them up. ACO taxa whose Colombian population eBird now calls by another name are remapped in aco_to_ebird.json instead (whole-species remap, same ACO record). `renamed`: one-off old slug -> new slug for those remaps; `build` carries `photos`/`sounds`/`texts` of the old data/species/<old>.json over to the new slug when `carry` is true (the old photos show the Colombian bird); otherwise the new slug waits for the CI `photos upload` run. Entries can be dropped once CI has refilled the new slugs.

Dacnis egregia.note: Yellow-tufted Dacnis, split from Black-faced Dacnis (D. lineata) in eBird/Clements: the population west of the Andes and in the Magdalena Valley (route: Pacific Nariño, Huila, Chicaque). D. lineata in the narrow sense is the Amazonian bird east of the Andes (Putumayo).

Grallaria alticola.note: Boyaca Antpitta, split from Tawny Antpitta (G. quitensis) by IOC (July 2023) and Clements (October 2023): Eastern Andes of Colombia (route: Chingaza, Sumapaz, the other Bogotá sites). G. quitensis stays for the Central Andes and Nariño (Bordoncillo, La Cocha). Not split by SACC/ACO and not in Chaparro-Herrera et al. 2024; `endemic` follows the Clements range (Eastern Andes of Colombia only).

Xenops mexicanus.note: Northern Plain-Xenops, split from Plain Xenops (X. minutus, now the Atlantic Forest bird) in eBird/Clements 2025: Mexico to western Colombia and the Magdalena valley, western Ecuador (route: Pacific Nariño, Maragrícola). The ACO taxon itself is remapped to Amazonian Plain-Xenops X. genibarbis (east of the Andes, Putumayo).

Formicivora intermedia.note: Northern White-fringed Antwren, split from White-fringed Antwren (F. grisea) in eBird/Clements: Caribbean lowlands, Magdalena valley, Panama and Venezuela (route: Chicaque). F. grisea in the narrow sense (Southern White-fringed Antwren) remains the bird of eastern Colombia (Guainía, Vaupés, Casanare; per eBird records by department, GBIF eBird dataset).

Setophaga aestiva.note: Northern Yellow Warbler, split from Yellow Warbler in eBird/Clements 2025: breeds in North America, winters south to northern South America; the boreal migrant of the ACO record (route: Bogotá, Huila, Putumayo, the Andes). S. petechia in the narrow sense is the resident Mangrove Yellow Warbler of the coasts (route: Tumaco, Playa del Morro).

Chlorothraupis frenata.note: Yellow-lored Tanager, split from Carmiol's Tanager (C. carmioli) in eBird/Clements: east slope of the Andes from Colombia to Bolivia (route: Putumayo, La Isla Escondida). C. carmioli in the narrow sense reaches Colombia only in the far northwest (3 records in Chocó; per eBird records by department, GBIF eBird dataset).

Automolus virgatus.note: Western Woodhaunter, split from Striped Woodhaunter (A. subulatus) in eBird/Clements: Costa Rica to western Colombia and Ecuador (route: Pacific Nariño). A. subulatus in the narrow sense (Eastern Woodhaunter) is the Amazonian bird (route: Putumayo).

Myiobius sulphureipygius.note: Sulphur-rumped Flycatcher, split from Whiskered Flycatcher (M. barbatus) in eBird/Clements: southern Mexico to western Colombia and western Ecuador (route: Pacific Nariño). M. barbatus in the narrow sense is the Amazonian bird east of the Andes.

Tunchiornis ferrugineifrons.note: Rufous-fronted Greenlet, split from Tawny-crowned Greenlet in eBird/Clements 2025: western Amazonia (route: Putumayo, La Isla Escondida). T. ochraceiceps in the narrow sense (Ochre-crowned Greenlet) is the bird west of the Andes (Chocó to western Ecuador).

Pachyramphus salvini.note: Cryptic Becard, split from Black-and-white Becard (P. albogriseus) in eBird/Clements: western Ecuador and northwest Peru to southwest Colombia; all Colombian eBird records are from Nariño (route: Pacific Nariño). P. albogriseus stays for the rest of Colombia (per eBird records by department, GBIF eBird dataset).

Furnarius cinnamomeus.note: Pacific Hornero, split from Pale-legged Hornero (F. leucopus) in eBird/Clements: Pacific lowlands of southwest Colombia, Ecuador and northwest Peru (route: Tumaco, Maragrícola, Km 42). F. leucopus in the narrow sense is Amazonian (Amazonas); Caribbean Hornero F. longirostris (north Colombia) is not on the route (per eBird records by department, GBIF eBird dataset).

Polioptila bilineata.note: White-browed Gnatcatcher, split from Tropical Gnatcatcher (P. plumbea) in eBird/Clements: Mexico to western Colombia and western Ecuador/Peru (route: Pacific Nariño and coast). P. plumbea in the narrow sense is the bird of the Andes valleys, the Caribbean and the east (per eBird records by department, GBIF eBird dataset).

Tolmomyias viridiceps.note: Olive-faced Flatbill, split from Yellow-breasted Flatbill (T. flaviventris) in eBird/Clements: western Amazonia (route: Putumayo). T. flaviventris in the narrow sense (Ochre-lored Flatbill) is the bird of the llanos and the Caribbean (per eBird records by department, GBIF eBird dataset).

Cryptopipo litae.note: Choco Manakin, split from Green Manakin (C. holochlora) in eBird/Clements: eastern Panama to western Ecuador (route: Pacific Nariño). C. holochlora in the narrow sense is the bird of the east slope and Amazonia (route: Putumayo) (per eBird records by department, GBIF eBird dataset).

Ocreatus peruanus.note: Peruvian Racket-tail, split from Booted Racket-tail (O. underwoodii) in eBird/Clements: east slope of the Andes from southern Colombia to Peru; Colombian eBird records are almost all from Putumayo (route: Mocoa area). O. underwoodii (White-booted Racket-tail) stays for the rest of the Andes (per eBird records by department, GBIF eBird dataset).

Myiopagis parambae.note: Choco Elaenia, split from Gray Elaenia (M. caniceps, now the Atlantic Forest bird) in eBird/Clements: eastern Panama to western Ecuador (route: Km 42, Maragrícola). The ACO taxon itself is remapped to Amazonian Elaenia M. cinerea (east of the Andes, Putumayo).
